entries.heading: What percolation is
entries.text: A cup of coffee is a random medium. Water finds its way through a packed bed of grounds because some channels are open and others are blocked, and the path it takes is decided by the geometry of the bed rather than by any randomness in the water. Broadbent and Hammersley put this picture into mathematics in 1957 and called it percolation , after the Latin percolare , to seep through. Their point was philosophical as much as technical: in diffusion theory the medium is fixed and the walking particle is random; in percolation the medium is random and the flow through it is completely determined once the medium is drawn. That single inversion turns out to generate an entire field. Declare each site or each bond of a graph open with probability p, independently, and ask a yes/no question: is there an infinite connected component of open elements? The answer changes qualitatively at one value of p. Around that value the geometry becomes scale invariant, and the quantities that describe it obey power laws whose exponents do not depend on the microscopic details of the graph. This is a phase transition with no temperature, no energy and no Hamiltonian — only connectivity.

entries.heading: The model in one paragraph
entries.text: Let G=(V,E) be a countably infinite, locally finite, connected graph, and let 0 V be a distinguished origin. Attach to every site (site percolation) or every bond (bond percolation) an independent Bernoulli variable with mean p. The open elements form a random subgraph; its connected components are the open clusters . Write C 0 for the cluster containing the origin, and define Everything else in this atlas is a refinement of these two lines. The function is the order parameter, p c is the critical probability, and the interesting statements are about what happens as p p c and as p p c.

entries.heading: Six observables
entries.text: Six quantities carry almost all of the theory. Their definitions are worth fixing once, because different communities normalise them differently and half of the confusion in the literature is bookkeeping. Percolation probability. (p)= {P} p(0 ). Two-point function. p(x,y)= {P} p(x y), with p(x)= p(0,x). This is the connectivity kernel; on a transitive graph it depends only on x-y. Cluster-size distribution. n(p)= {P} p( C 0 =n) for n< , and = . Susceptibility. (p)= {E} p C 0 = {n 1} n\, n(p), with the convention that (p)= when (p) 0. This is the mean size of the cluster at the origin, including the infinite cluster. It diverges as p p c and is infinite above p c; that divergence is the cleanest numerical signal of criticality. Correlation length. (p)^{-1}= {n }- 1n p(0,n e 1), the exponential rate of decay of connectivity along a coordinate axis. It diverges as p p c from either side. Crossing probability. On a finite box , (p)= {P} p( {open left–right crossing of } ). This is the observable that finite-size studies actually measure, because it is an indicator with a sharp threshold in L and no need for an infinite lattice. A sixth quantity, the cluster number density n s(p)= {P} p( C 0 =s)/s per site, is the natural object for scaling theory; it appears in Chapter 6 and is the reason exists.

entries.heading: Why one parameter is enough
entries.text: It is tempting to think that a model this poor in structure cannot produce anything universal. The opposite is true, and the reason is a separation of scales. Near p c the correlation length is enormous compared with the lattice spacing, so the microscopic arrangement of edges is averaged over many times before a cluster can decide whether it is infinite. Universality is the statement that in this limit only a few features of the microscopic model survive: the dimension, and the symmetries that constrain the large-scale geometry (rotation and reflection invariance, and for percolation the colour symmetry between open and closed). The price of this economy is that the model is critical at a single point and therefore numerically delicate: at p c the relevant scale is the system size itself, finite-size effects are power-law rather than exponential, and naive fits give biased exponents. Chapter 11 is devoted to doing this correctly.

entries.heading: Five layers of the picture
entries.text: The subject is usually taught as a stack, and it helps to see the whole stack at once. 1. Local connectivity. For fixed p, the box contains many clusters of many sizes; the size distribution is the object of study. 2. A threshold. On an infinite transitive graph there is a single p c (0,1) at which the qualitative behaviour changes. Existence is easy; locating it is hard. 3. Critical scaling. Near p c, observables behave as powers of p-p c or of the system size, with exponents that are universal. 4. Geometric limit. In two dimensions the scaling limit of the critical clusters is conformally invariant, and the interfaces converge to SLE 6. This is the only dimension in which the limit is understood in full. 5. Translation. Ising, Potts, random graphs, epidemics, resistor networks, error-correcting codes and network robustness can all be written as percolation problems, sometimes exactly and sometimes only as analogies. Separating the two is a recurring theme of this atlas.

entries.heading: Landmarks
entries.text: Three results orient a newcomer. On the square lattice, bond percolation has p c=1/2 exactly (Kesten 1980). On the triangular lattice, site percolation has p c=1/2 exactly, a fact with a short star–triangle proof (Chapter 4). For the triangular lattice and its star–triangle relatives, the two-dimensional critical exponents are known exactly: =5/36, =43/18, =4/3, =91/5, =5/24, d f=91/48. In three dimensions no threshold or exponent is known exactly; the best numerical values are 0.4181, 0.8764, d f 2.5229, with error bars in the last quoted digit. Above six dimensions the mean-field values = =1, =1/2, =2, =0, d f=4 are expected; they are proved for d 11 (Chapter 8), and at d=6 the exponents are mean-field with logarithmic corrections. The gap between the exact results and the numerical middle is the honest shape of the field: exact in two dimensions, rigorous for d 11, numerical in between.

entries.heading: How to read this atlas
entries.text: If you want intuition, read this chapter and Chapter 4, then open the Lattice lab and watch a crossing probability sharpen as L grows. If you want the rigorous core, read Chapters 3–5 in order (monotonicity and existence, duality and exact thresholds, sharpness and uniqueness), then Chapter 7 for the two-dimensional limit. If you are here for networks or epidemics, read Chapters 10, 22 and 23 in that order: degree distributions, generating functions and the SIR mapping. Chapter 11 is the numerical methodology that keeps an application from producing a plausible but wrong threshold. If you want to check a claim, every theorem that is proved in full is marked ★, every numerical value carries its source and precision, and Chapter 14 indexes the proofs, records the corrections made in this edition, and lists the sources used throughout.

entries.heading: A short history
entries.text: The history of percolation is unusually clean: a definite starting paper, a definite golden age, and a definite resolution in two dimensions. What follows is a timeline with the primary sources attached, so that each claim can be traced.

entries.heading: 1957: the founding paper
entries.text: S. R. Broadbent and J. M. Hammersley, Percolation processes: I. Crystals and mazes , Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 53(3), 629–641. The paper introduces the model, distinguishes it from diffusion, and poses the question that defines the field: does a critical probability exist? Their examples are a gas diffusing through a random array of blocked channels, a disease spreading through an orchard, and fluid seeping through a porous solid. The vocabulary — open, closed, cluster, percolation probability — is theirs. The companion note, J. M. Hammersley, Percolation processes: II. The connective constant , same volume, 642–645, treats the one-dimensional chain and the Bethe lattice. On a tree of degree z the threshold is 1/(z-1), the first exact nontrivial value, and it remains the geometric incarnation of mean-field theory.

entries.heading: 1960–1980: the square lattice
entries.text: T. E. Harris, A lower bound for the critical probability in a certain percolation process , Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 56 (1960), 13–20, proves (1/2)=0 on {Z}^2, i.e. p c 1/2. The argument combines the planar duality of open and closed crossings with the colour symmetry at p=1/2; both ideas become permanent tools. M. F. Sykes and J. W. Essam, Exact critical percolation probabilities for site and bond problems in two dimensions , J. Math. Phys. 5 (1964), 1117, introduce the matching method and obtain closed forms for the triangular and honeycomb bond thresholds. Their route runs through the star–triangle transformation; the algebra is reproduced, correctly, in Chapter 4, where the derivation is checked step by step. L. Russo, A note on percolation , Z. Wahrsch. Verw. Gebiete 43 (1978), 39–48, and P. D. Seymour and D. J. A. Welsh, Percolation probabilities on the square lattice , Ann. Discrete Math. 3 (1978), 227–245, independently prove the box-crossing inequalities that make two-dimensional percolation tractable. The RSW lemma is the engine behind almost every rigorous two-dimensional result, including Kesten's theorem two years later. H. Kesten, The critical probability of bond percolation on the square lattice equals 1/2 , Comm. Math. Phys. 74 (1980), 41–59, closes the gap. The proof is long and technical. Bollobás and Riordan (2006) give a substantially shorter route using sharp-threshold technology.

entries.heading: 1970s–1980s: critical phenomena
entries.text: The translation of percolation into the language of critical phenomena is associated with P.-G. de Gennes, On a relation between percolation theory and the elasticity of gels , J. Physique Lettres 37 (1976), L1–L2, and with the Stauffer school. D. Stauffer and A. Aharony, Introduction to Percolation Theory (Taylor & Francis, 2nd ed. 1994), fixed the notation , , , , that everyone now uses, and taught a generation to fit exponents from Monte Carlo data — sometimes too optimistically, a habit that Chapter 11 tries to correct. On the rigorous side, H. Kesten, Percolation Theory for Mathematicians (Birkhäuser, 1982), established the subject as a branch of probability. M. Aizenman and D. J. Barsky, Sharpness of the phase transition in percolation models , Comm. Math. Phys. 108 (1987), 489–526, proved exponential decay below p c; M. V. Menshikov proved the corresponding results independently (1986–87). The Burton–Keane uniqueness theorem (1989) completed the qualitative picture of the supercritical phase.

entries.heading: 1986–1992: high dimensions and conformal field theory
entries.text: M. Aizenman and R. Fernández, On the critical behavior of the magnetization in high dimensional Ising models , J. Stat. Phys. 44 (1986), 393, proved mean-field behaviour for the high-dimensional Ising model with the random-current representation. T. Hara and G. Slade, Mean-field critical behaviour for percolation in high dimensions , Comm. Math. Phys. 128 (1990), 333–391, developed the lace expansion for percolation and proved the corresponding result in sufficiently high dimension. The lace expansion is non-perturbative and remains the only rigorous route to critical exponents above the upper critical dimension. The current threshold for nearest-neighbour bond percolation is d 11 (Fitzner and van der Hofstad, 2017), building on Hara and Slade's d 19 result and later refinements of the expansion. In parallel, J. L. Cardy, Critical percolation in finite geometries , J. Phys. A 25 (1992), L201, used conformal field theory to predict the exact crossing probability of a rectangle. R. Langlands, P. Pouliot and Y. Saint-Aubin, Conformal invariance in two-dimensional percolation , Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 30 (1994), 1–61, checked it numerically and attributed the underlying conjecture to Aizenman.

entries.heading: 2001: the two-dimensional revolution
entries.text: S. Smirnov, Critical percolation in the plane: conformal invariance, Cardy's formula, scaling limits , C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris Sér. I Math. 333 (2001), 239–244, proved Cardy's formula for critical site percolation on the triangular lattice. The proof is short enough to be read in an afternoon and deep enough to have changed the subject: it identifies the continuum limit of the exploration interface as a conformally invariant object. G. F. Lawler, O. Schramm and W. Werner, Values of Brownian intersection exponents I, II , Acta Math. 187 (2001), 237–273 and 275–308, and their subsequent work, identified the interface limit as SLE 6 and derived the exact exponent set. The chain Cardy → Smirnov → SLE is the most complete solution of a critical model in two dimensions after the Ising model.

entries.heading: 2000s: networks
entries.text: R. Cohen, K. Erez, D. ben-Avraham and S. Havlin, Resilience of the Internet to random breakdowns , Phys. Rev. Lett. 85 (2000), 4626, and D. S. Callaway, M. E. J. Newman, S. H. Strogatz and D. J. Watts, Network robustness and fragility: percolation on random graphs , Phys. Rev. Lett. 85 (2000), 5468, brought percolation into network science. The Molloy–Reed criterion, already implicit in M. Molloy and B. Reed, A critical point for random graphs with a given degree sequence , Random Structures & Algorithms 6 (1995), 161–180, became the standard tool. S. V. Buldyrev, R. Parshani, G. Paul, H. E. Stanley and S. Havlin, Catastrophic cascade of failures in interdependent networks , Nature 464 (2010), 1025–1028, showed that coupling two networks turns a continuous transition into a discontinuous one. The result is the clearest example of a percolation transition whose type is a design variable.

entries.heading: 2010s–2020s
entries.text: The rigorous high-dimensional programme advanced to d 11 and produced a proof that the triangle condition holds there; the three-dimensional problem remains numerical. Higher-order percolation on simplicial complexes, percolation on temporal and multilayer networks, and the percolation threshold of quantum error-correcting codes are the active frontier. Chapter 13 lists the open problems in the order in which they look tractable. Two dating conventions are worth flagging. The Aizenman–Barsky sharpness paper is often cited as 1986 because it circulated in preprint form that year; the journal volume is 1987. And the current high-dimensional threshold is d 11, not the older d 19 that still appears in secondary sources. Chapter 14 records both corrections.

entries.chapterTitle: Monotonicity and the existence of a threshold
entries.heading: Monotonicity and the existence of a threshold
entries.text: Before any threshold can be computed it has to exist. This chapter proves that it does, and along the way introduces the two inequalities that every later argument uses: positive association (FKG) and the coupling monotonicity of . The proofs are elementary; they are written out because the rest of the atlas leans on them.

entries.chapterTitle: Monotonicity and the existence of a threshold
entries.heading: 3.6 What monotonicity does not give
entries.text: Monotonicity is a statement about changing p with the graph fixed . It says nothing about changing the graph. Adding edges lowers p c; subdividing every edge replaces an open bond of probability p by two in series and therefore moves the bond threshold to {p c}, which raises it. The intuition "more connections, lower threshold" is reliable for edge inclusion, not for arbitrary graph operations. Chapter 11 lists the resulting traps. A second limitation: FKG is an inequality, not an identity. It gives the sign of correlations but not their size, and for quantitative work (for instance, the RSW constants) one needs the actual crossing estimates, which are much finer.

entries.chapterTitle: Duality, matching, and the exact thresholds
entries.heading: Duality, matching, and the exact thresholds
entries.text: Planar duality is the principal tool that produces exact thresholds, and it does so in two steps: first it converts a statement about open crossings into a statement about closed crossings, then a symmetry argument pins the critical point to the self-dual value. On the square lattice the two steps give p c=1/2. On the triangular and honeycomb lattices a second ingredient, the star–triangle transformation, is needed. The derivation is in Section 4.4; the algebraic shortcut that looks plausible but gives the wrong root is explained there too.

entries.chapterTitle: Duality, matching, and the exact thresholds
entries.heading: 4.1 The matching graph and the crossing lemma
entries.text: Definition 4.1. Let G be a graph embedded in the plane with locally finite faces. The matching graph G^ has one vertex in each face of G, and one edge crossing each edge of G, joining the two faces adjacent to it. G is self-dual if G^ G as planar graphs. The square lattice is self-dual; the triangular and honeycomb lattices are matched to each other. Lemma 4.2 (crossing duality, ★). Let n=[-n,n]^2 and let n^ be the matching square. For every bond configuration on n, exactly one of the following holds: - A: there is an open left–right crossing of n; - B^ : there is a closed top–bottom crossing of n^ . Proof. Color every bond of n open or closed, and draw the dual bond of n^ closed when the primal bond is open, open when the primal bond is closed. The two families of bonds therefore form a pair of complementary planar duals. At most one. Suppose A and B^ both hold. The open left–right path P and the closed top–bottom dual path Q must cross at some primal edge e: the paths intersect as curves in the plane, and a crossing of a horizontal primal path with a vertical dual path occurs exactly at an edge. At that edge e is open (because P uses it) and closed (because Q uses its dual), a contradiction. At least one. Suppose A fails. Consider the set S of primal vertices reachable from the left side by open paths. Its edge boundary consists of closed edges: an edge from S to S^c cannot be open, or the endpoint would be in S. Walk along the boundary of S from the top of the box to the bottom; the duals of the boundary edges form a closed dual path joining the top and bottom sides of n^ . This is B^ . (If S is empty the whole left side is closed, and the dual path runs along the left boundary.) The lemma is the two-dimensional replacement for the absence of a "monotone coupling" in higher dimensions. Everything exact in d=2 starts here.

entries.chapterTitle: Duality, matching, and the exact thresholds
entries.heading: 4.2 Why the self-dual point is $1/2$
entries.text: Proposition 4.3 (★). For bond percolation on {Z}^2 at p=1/2, The convergence is not exact at finite n. Exact enumeration at p=1/2 gives 3/4 on the 2 2 vertex box, 43/64=0.671875 on the 3 3 box, and 82623/131072=0.63036 on the 4 4 box. The sequence decreases slowly towards 1/2; the identity is asymptotic, and it must not be used as a per-size calibration. Proof sketch. Lemma 4.2 gives for every p and n. At p=1/2, colour exchange turns the closed top–bottom crossing B n^ of the dual box into an open top–bottom crossing. The dual box has side 2n faces, while A n lives on a (2n+1) (2n+1) vertex box; the two crossing probabilities are therefore not equal at finite n, but their difference is a boundary term that vanishes as n . RSW bounds both sequences away from 0 and 1, so every subsequential limit exists and is bounded away from the endpoints. The boundary term forces any such limit to satisfy 2 =1, hence =1/2; the full sequence converges to the same value. A complete proof identifies the limit through the Harris–Kesten theorem or Cardy's formula. The finite-size values are the reason the benchmark in data/benchmarks.json reports the crossing rate with its sample count rather than asserting 1/2. At L=32,64,128 the recorded rates at p=1/2 are 0.5275, 0.5375 and 0.505; they approach 1/2 but are not equal to it at any of these sizes. What Proposition 4.3 does not give is p c=1/2. It says that p=1/2 is a fixed point of the duality in the infinite-volume limit, not that it is the critical point. A model could in principle have a first-order transition elsewhere and still satisfy the limiting identity. Closing that gap is the Harris–Kesten theorem.

entries.chapterTitle: Duality, matching, and the exact thresholds
entries.heading: 4.3 Harris–Kesten: the architecture
entries.text: Theorem 4.4 (Harris 1960; Kesten 1980). For bond percolation on {Z}^2, p c=1/2. The proof has two halves that use different machinery. Lower half, p c 1/2 (Harris). Suppose (1/2) 0. Then there is an infinite open cluster with positive probability, and by the uniqueness theorem (Theorem 5.3, which does not depend on the value of p c) it is almost surely unique. A standard consequence of uniqueness plus positive density is that the probability of an open left–right crossing of n tends to 1 as n : the infinite cluster has positive density, so it meets both sides of a large box, and the crossing event fails only if the cluster is disconnected inside the box, an event of exponentially small probability. This contradicts the limit in Proposition 4.3, which forces the crossing probability to tend to 1/2. Hence (1/2)=0 and p c 1/2. The step from uniqueness to "crossing probability tends to one" is the only non-elementary ingredient; it is proved in Grimmett's Percolation , Chapter 8, and it is where the hypothesis of amenability enters. Everything else in the lower half is Proposition 4.3. Upper half, p c 1/2 (Kesten). The engine is the RSW inequality. Theorem 4.5 (Russo 1978; Seymour–Welsh 1978). There is a constant 0 such that for all p and all n, The implication is the non-trivial direction of RSW: a square crossing with probability at least one half forces a long rectangle to be crossed with a probability bounded below independently of n. The proof is a coarse-graining argument. Place three overlapping n n squares along the long rectangle. A left–right crossing of the long rectangle can be assembled from crossings of the three squares, and FKG turns a lower bound on the probability of each square crossing into a lower bound on the probability of the assembly. The constant depends only on the value 1/2, not on n. With RSW in hand, Kesten's argument has three steps. Take p=1/2+ . First, duality and the Harris lower bound p c 1/2 show that a closed dual crossing of a long rectangle has probability tending to zero; equivalently, the primal crossing probability of a long rectangle tends to one. Second, RSW gives a uniform lower bound for crossings of rectangles of every scale. Third, the standard ladder (renormalisation) argument converts these scale-uniform bounds into an infinite open path with positive probability, so (1/2+ ) 0. Hence p c 1/2+ for every 0. The second and third steps are where the proof is long; the first is the part that uses duality at the critical point. Remark 4.6. The proof has been simplified repeatedly. The route in Bollobás and Riordan (2006) uses the Friedgut–Kalai sharp-threshold theorem; it is conceptually cleaner but relies on a different heavy result. No proof is short. What matters for this atlas is the structure: duality gives the fixed point, RSW gives rigidity at the fixed point, and rigidity upgrades the fixed point to the critical point.

entries.chapterTitle: Duality, matching, and the exact thresholds
entries.heading: 4.4 Matching pairs, the star–triangle transformation, and the corrected cubic
entries.text: Theorem 4.7 (matching relation). Let G,G^ be a matching pair of periodic planar graphs, both amenable. Then Proof idea. A configuration of G and its colour-exchanged dual configuration on G^ are complementary in the sense of Lemma 4.2. The planar separation argument upgrades the finite-box statement to the infinite one: G has no infinite open cluster if and only if G^ has an infinite closed -cluster. Translating "closed -cluster at density 1-p" into "open cluster at density q" gives the identity. The amenability hypothesis is needed to exclude the possibility that both sides fail to percolate with positive probability. For the pair (triangular T, honeycomb H) this gives one equation. The second equation is the star–triangle identity, and it is here that the algebra must be done carefully. Theorem 4.8 (Sykes–Essam 1964; ★ algebra). For bond percolation, Derivation. Work on the triangular lattice at its critical point p=p c(T), and let q=1-p be the density of closed bonds, which by the matching relation is the critical density of the honeycomb. A star (a vertex with three bonds to three outer vertices) with bond probability q connects all three outer vertices pairwise exactly when all three bonds are open, an event of probability q^3. A triangle with bond probability p connects its three vertices pairwise whenever at least two of its three bonds are open, an event of probability The star–triangle transformation identifies these two three-terminal networks at the critical point, so Substituting q=1-p gives The cubic has three real roots, 2 (10^ ), 2 (50^ ) and -2 (70^ ); only the first lies in (0,1), so Numerical check: with p=0.34729635533386066, q^3=0.2780661432813856 and 3p^2-2p^3=0.2780661432813855, agreeing to the last bit of double precision. Why a plausible shortcut fails. A tempting but incorrect route equates the triangle connectivity to the star density : 3p^2-2p^3=1-p. That is not the three-terminal connectivity of a star; the star connects all three outer vertices only when all three of its bonds are open, which has probability (1-p)^3. The wrong equation gives the cubic which has the root p=1/2 and two roots outside (0,1). It therefore "predicts" the bond threshold 1/2, which is actually the site threshold of the triangular lattice. The numerical difference is large (0.3473 versus 0.5), and the fact that both numbers are often quoted in the same table is precisely why provenance matters. The correct cubic gives 2 10^ , in agreement with Sykes and Essam (1964). Remark 4.9 (the status of the Y–Δ step). The identity q^3=3p^2-2p^3 is not a distributional equality of a single star and a single triangle: the two networks have different cycle structure and different connectivity distributions for the three boundary vertices. It is the q { {RC}} 1 limit of the Yang–Baxter (star–triangle) relation for the random-cluster model, used at the level of the three-terminal connectivity function; q { {RC}} is the random-cluster cluster weight, not the closed-bond density q used above. Treating it as a local identity to be applied triangle by triangle is a common error and produces nonsense; it is a critical-point identity, and its rigorous justification for the bond problem is the content of the Sykes–Essam matching argument, later made rigorous by Wierman.

entries.chapterTitle: Duality, matching, and the exact thresholds
entries.heading: 4.5 The triangular site threshold
entries.text: Theorem 4.10. For site percolation on the triangular lattice, p c=1/2. Argument (★ structure). The triangular lattice is fully triangulated, so every face is a triangle and the matching graph of the site problem is the honeycomb with the roles of vertices and faces exchanged. The star–triangle transformation now acts on sites : a site of the triangular lattice with its six neighbours is dual to a hexagon of the honeycomb whose six sites are its duals. At density p, the probability that a site is open equals the probability that the corresponding hexagon is "blocked", and the fully triangulated structure makes the two events complementary. Hence and the self-dual point of the transformation is p=1/2. The rigorous version is due to Wierman (1981); see Grimmett (1999), §11.9, for a complete account. Menshikov and Aizenman–Barsky prove sharpness of the phase transition, not the numerical value of this threshold; the two sets of results are often conflated in secondary accounts. Corollary 4.11. If a planar graph G contains the triangular lattice as a subgraph, then p c^{ {site}}(G) 1/2, because adding edges and vertices cannot increase the threshold. There is no universal lower bound of this kind for arbitrary planar graphs: adding edges to the triangular lattice lowers the threshold, and planar graphs that contain a triangular sublattice can sit below 1/2.

entries.chapterTitle: Duality, matching, and the exact thresholds
entries.heading: 4.7 What not to infer
entries.text: The table invites a false pattern: thresholds decrease as the coordination number increases. The pattern is real on average but useless quantitatively. The kagome lattice has z=4 and site threshold 0.6527, while the square lattice has the same z=4 and site threshold 0.5927; the difference comes from the ring structure, not the degree. Formulas of the type p c 2/z or the Galam–Mauger interpolation reproduce the table to within a few percent on some lattices and fail badly on others. They are not theorems and should never be used to "predict" a threshold that matters. Chapter 11 lists the measurement traps that follow from this.

entries.heading: Sharpness and uniqueness
entries.text: Two theorems turn the definition of p c into a usable theory. The first says that below p c connectivity decays exponentially, so "no infinite cluster" is a strong statement about every length scale, not just about infinity. The second says that above p c there is exactly one infinite cluster, so "percolating" is a property of the whole system rather than of a lucky component. Both hold on {Z}^d; the uniqueness theorem extends to transitive amenable graphs, while the sharpness theorem is stated here for the lattice. The proofs use completely different ideas.

entries.heading: 5.1 Exponential decay
entries.text: Theorem 5.1 (Aizenman–Barsky 1987; Menshikov 1986). Let G= {Z}^d. For every p

entries.heading: 5.2 Uniqueness of the infinite cluster
entries.text: Theorem 5.3 (Burton–Keane 1989). Let G be a transitive amenable graph. For every p, Proof sketch. The argument has three ingredients. Ergodicity. The number N( ) of infinite open clusters is a translation-invariant measurable function, so it is almost surely constant on each ergodic component. On a transitive amenable graph the Bernoulli measure is ergodic under translations, hence N \{0,1,2, \} \{ \} is a constant almost surely. Finite energy. For a finite edge set F, let ^F be the configuration obtained from by opening every edge of F. Conditional on the configuration outside F, the probability of seeing any prescribed pattern on F is at least (p,1-p)^{ F } 0. In particular, if opening F would merge two infinite clusters of , then this merge happens with conditional probability bounded below by a constant depending only on F and p. No finite merge. Suppose N=k 2 almost surely. Two distinct infinite clusters cannot be joined by a finite set of edges without changing N, so for every finite F the event "opening F reduces N" has probability zero. But a configuration with k 2 infinite clusters has infinitely many finite sets F whose opening would merge two of them: take a large finite region meeting two of the clusters inside a single connected piece and shrink the connecting edge set until it is minimal. By finite energy and translation invariance, the probability that at least one such minimal F succeeds is positive, contradicting the previous sentence. The third step is the one that needs care, and it is where amenability enters: on a non-amenable graph the number of infinite clusters can genuinely be infinite (the 3-regular tree at p above the critical value has infinitely many infinite clusters, since distinct branches are independent). The complete proof is in Burton–Keane (1989); a textbook treatment is Grimmett (1999), §8.2. Corollary 5.4. For p p c, almost every vertex belongs to the unique infinite cluster or to a finite cluster, and for every choice of origin. In this regime the "percolating" event is translation invariant and has probability one conditionally on the origin being in the infinite cluster. The second corollary is what licenses the renormalisation arguments of Chapter 4: once (p) 0, one may speak of the infinite cluster and use its density as a macroscopic order parameter.

entries.heading: 5.3 Continuity at the critical point
entries.text: Theorem 5.5 (Kesten 1980; RSW). For bond percolation on {Z}^2, (p c)=0 and is continuous at p c. Moreover (p) as p p c. Proof idea. At p c, duality gives {P}(A n)+ {P}(B n^ )=1. RSW gives a uniform lower bound for the dual crossing probability {P}(B n^ ), hence a uniform upper bound {P}(A n) 1- for the primal crossing. If (p c) 0, then by uniqueness and positive density the crossing probability would tend to one, contradicting the uniform upper bound. Hence (p c)=0. Continuity follows from the same estimates: the probability that the origin is connected to distance n is bounded by a constant times the probability of a crossing of the annulus, which tends to zero as n uniformly for p p c. The result is special to two dimensions in its proof, not in its statement: in high dimensions continuity at p c is known as part of the lace-expansion theory; in the intermediate dimensions that include d=3,4,5 it remains open. The contrast is worth keeping in mind when reading numerical claims about the order parameter: a discontinuous jump at p c would be visible in a simulation as a plateau, and no such plateau has ever been seen in three dimensions, but "not seen" is not "proved absent".

entries.heading: 5.4 First-order transitions: the exception, not the rule
entries.text: The continuity of the Bernoulli transition is not a universal law of nature; it is a theorem about independent percolation. Three mechanisms produce discontinuous transitions, and each is treated later in this atlas: - Correlated percolation. Long-range positive correlations can produce a jump in the order parameter; the random-cluster model with q large has a first-order transition for q above a dimension-dependent threshold. - k-core percolation. Requiring local redundancy rather than mere connectivity changes the transition to first order at k 3 (Chapter 10). - Coupled networks. Two networks that depend on each other's giant component generate a cascade with a discontinuous jump (Chapter 10). The lesson is that "percolation is continuous" is a statement about the independence of the bonds, not about connectivity as such. Any application that couples percolation to another dynamical process must check which regime it is in before assuming a continuous transition.

entries.heading: 5.5 What sharpness buys
entries.text: Three practical consequences follow from this chapter and are used repeatedly. First, the finite-size scaling ansatz of Chapter 6 is justified: below p c all lengths are controlled by , and above p c the infinite cluster is unique and dense, so the only remaining scale at p c is the system size. Second, the numerical detection of p c by susceptibility divergence is legitimate, and its error bars can be estimated from the scaling of with L. Third, the uniqueness theorem makes the "giant component" language of network science consistent with the lattice language: on a large finite graph, above the threshold there is one component of size (N), and the second largest is o(N). The statement is asymptotic; on a graph of 10^4 vertices the second largest component can still be large enough to matter, which is a recurring source of confusion in applied papers.

entries.heading: Exponents, scaling relations, and universality
entries.text: At p c the correlation length diverges and the system loses its only length scale. Everything that remains is a power law, and the exponents of those power laws are the quantitative content of universality. This chapter defines them, derives the relations among them, and separates the exponents that are known exactly from those that are only known numerically.

entries.heading: 6.1 Definitions
entries.text: As p p c (for ) and p p c from either side (for the rest): The cluster-number density is n s(p)= {P} p( C 0 =s)/s; at criticality n s s^{- } with =2+1/ . The fractal dimension d f describes the mass–radius relation of a critical cluster, the spectral dimension d s describes the return probability of a random walk on it, and d { } describes the shortest-path (chemical) distance. The one-arm probability is the chance that the origin is connected to the boundary of a box of side n at p c: It scales as n^{- / }. This identity is used constantly as a fingerprint. The two-dimensional value is n^{-5/48}=n^{-0.10417 }; a frequently seen n^{-2/3} is not consistent with the exponent set and is a useful diagnostic of a copied formula.

entries.heading: 6.4 Why the upper critical dimension is six
entries.text: The upper critical dimension is the dimension above which mean-field exponents become exact. For self-avoiding walks it is four; for percolation it is six. The difference is a counting argument about loops, and it is worth doing carefully because the counting is easy to state too loosely. Consider the two-point function at criticality. In mean-field theory (x) x ^{-(d-2)}, so its Fourier transform behaves as (k) k ^{-2}. The corrections to mean-field theory are organised by the triangle (bubble) diagram which counts three paths joining two branch points, i.e. a theta graph. In Fourier space this is (k)^3\,d^dk k ^{-6}\,d^dk, which converges exactly when d 6. When it converges, the lace expansion can be organised as a convergent series and the mean-field exponents follow; when it diverges, the series does not control the critical behaviour. The same counting in position space: each of the three paths contributes a factor of dimension d-2, and the two branch points contribute 2d; the diagram is finite when 3(d-2) 2d, i.e. d 6. For a self-avoiding walk the analogous diagram has two paths and one loop, 2(d-2) d, giving d c=4. The extra path is what raises six above four. At d=6 exactly, k ^{-6} diverges logarithmically, and the mean-field picture survives only with logarithmic corrections to the scaling forms. The exponents are the mean-field ones, but the amplitudes carry logarithms; the coefficients require a separate renormalisation-group calculation.

entries.heading: 6.5 The status of universality
entries.text: Universality is the claim that the exponents depend only on the dimension (and on symmetries), not on the lattice. Its status differs sharply by dimension. Two dimensions: theorem for the triangular lattice and its star–triangle relatives. For critical site percolation on the triangular lattice, the scaling limit is conformally invariant and the interfaces converge to SLE 6 (Chapter 7), which fixes the exponents. The same exponent set is expected on every periodic planar lattice in the same universality class, but conformal invariance of the scaling limit for a general planar lattice is still a conjecture, supported by extensive numerics. This is the most important open problem in the rigorous two-dimensional theory and is discussed in Chapter 13. Above six dimensions: theorem. Lace expansion proves mean-field behaviour for d 11 for nearest-neighbour bond percolation (Fitzner–van der Hofstad 2017), with Hara and Slade's earlier d 19 threshold (1990). The result includes the values = =1, =1/2, =2, =0, d f=4 and the behaviour (p)=c 1(p-p c)+c 2(p-p c)^2+O((p-p c)^3) for p p c, with c 1 0; is C^2 on (p c,1] and has one-sided right derivatives at p c. Three to five dimensions: no proof. The exponents in the table for d=3,4,5 are numerical. They are extremely well constrained — the relations of Section 6.3 hold to the quoted precision, and independent methods (Monte Carlo, conformal bootstrap where applicable, functional renormalisation group) agree — but they are not theorems. Any statement that "the three-dimensional percolation exponents are known" is, strictly, a statement about numerics. Bethe lattice: exact. The mean-field exponents are computed exactly in Chapter 8 by solving the branching-process recursion. The Bethe lattice is the d limit and the reference point against which the finite-dimensional numbers are compared.

entries.heading: 6.6 Reading exponents off data
entries.text: The exponents are defined as limits as 0 and L , and neither limit is available in a simulation. The practical consequence is that a naive log–log fit gives an effective exponent that drifts with the fit window. A susceptibility fit at a single size can look stable while its slope changes by a factor of two across the critical region; Chapter 11 explains how to detect the drift and what to report instead. The correct procedure has three parts. Use a scaling ansatz with corrections to scaling, A(p,L)=L^{y} A ((p-p c)L^{1/ } ) (1+cL^{- } ); fit all sizes simultaneously; and report a confidence interval from resampling rather than a single number. The benchmark data in data/benchmarks.json is produced this way, and the fit residuals are part of the published record, not an afterthought.

entries.heading: Two dimensions: Cardy, Smirnov, SLE
entries.text: In two dimensions the critical interface is a curve, and curves have an infinite-dimensional symmetry group: the conformal maps. At the critical point, that symmetry is enough to determine the scaling limit of the triangular-lattice model. This chapter follows the chain from Cardy's 1992 conjecture to Smirnov's 2001 theorem to the SLE description of Lawler, Schramm and Werner, and records the exact exponent set that comes out.

entries.heading: 7.1 Why the interface is the right object
entries.text: At p c the open cluster of the origin is a fractal with d f=91/48 1.896, and its boundary is a random curve that fluctuates on every scale. Consider the exploration interface: start at a boundary point of a simply connected domain, and walk along the boundary between the open cluster touching one arc and the closed cluster touching the other. The walk is determined by the colouring, it can be generated without look-ahead, and its law is the object whose scaling limit we want. Two properties of this walk are inherited from the lattice and survive the continuum limit: - Domain Markov property. Conditioned on the interface up to time t, the law of the remaining configuration in the unexplored region is the same percolation law, with the boundary conditions transported by the interface. - Colour symmetry. At p=1/2 swapping open and closed leaves the law invariant. A random curve with these two properties and conformal invariance is an SLE; the parameter is fixed by locality, the continuum form of the domain Markov property together with colour symmetry. That gives =6.

entries.heading: 7.2 Smirnov's theorem
entries.text: Theorem 7.1 (Smirnov 2001). Let be a simply connected domain with four marked boundary points A,B,C,D in counterclockwise order, and let be a discretisation by the triangular lattice with mesh . For critical site percolation on , the probability that there is an open crossing from the arc AB to the arc CD has a limit as 0 which is conformally invariant, and for a rectangle of aspect ratio =H/W the limit is Cardy's formula. Proof architecture. The proof has four steps, and each is worth knowing because together they are the template for every later result of this kind. Step 1: three observables. For a point z in the domain, let H 1(z),H 2(z),H 3(z) be the probabilities that the interface from z exits through the three boundary arcs determined by the marked points. They sum to one, and each is a harmonic-type function of z. Step 2: discrete Cauchy–Riemann. On the triangular lattice the colour of a vertex determines the local move of the interface, and the three-colouring of the hexagonal dual makes the combination H 1+ H 2+ ^2H 3 (with =e^{2 i/3}) satisfy a discrete Cauchy–Riemann equation. This is the technical heart: the lattice is exactly the one on which the discrete holomorphic structure closes. Step 3: compactness. RSW estimates give uniform bounds on the oscillation of the H i at all scales, so the family is precompact and a subsequence converges. Step 4: identification. The limit is holomorphic, has the boundary values forced by the geometry, and is therefore unique. Cardy's formula is the solution of that boundary-value problem. Why the triangular lattice. The discrete holomorphicity in Step 2 uses the fact that the triangular lattice and its hexagonal matching graph fit together so that every face is a triangle, and the interface has exactly three local choices. It is the triangular face structure, not self-duality, that makes the argument close. For the square lattice, or for a general planar lattice, the corresponding discrete object is not known to converge; conformal invariance of the scaling limit is still a conjecture there, supported by very strong numerics. This is the central open problem of the rigorous two-dimensional theory.
