The implementation uses the same DSU and reports the trajectory as an exact function of the candidate sequence. The three algorithms share the four-language parity contract recorded in data/golden/algorithms-v3.json: Python and JavaScript generate the probes, and the C++ and Julia suites assert the same file. The Bernoulli core keeps its own contract in data/golden/parity.json. The correctness arguments are in Chapter 19, the instruments are laboratories 10–12, and the site's Algorithm reader links each invariant to the exact source file. Six further routines were added in the 4.x releases: Hoshen–Kopelman labelling, the Bethe fixed point, the configuration-model giant component, the SIR final size, the site-mode Newman–Ziff sweep and message passing. Of these, Hoshen–Kopelman, the Bethe fixed point, the configuration giant component, the SIR final size and message passing are deterministic; the site sweep consumes one random site order. The first four are described in Chapters 22–23, the site sweep is the site counterpart of §15.5, and message passing is the finite-graph form of the Bethe recursion in §22.5. All six have golden probes in the same algorithms-v3.json file.

entries.chapterTitle: Algorithms: from one sample to the whole curve
entries.heading: 15.9 Reading the implementations
entries.text: The JavaScript engine is the one the browser runs; the Python package is the readable reference; the C++ headers are the fast path; the Julia package is the typed path with the same public conventions. The edge order is fixed by build lattice, the random stream by docs/RNG.md, and the DSU by the pseudocode above. A change to any of the three is a breaking change: regenerate the goldens, bump the version, and record the correction in Chapter 14. The algorithms in this chapter are also the reason the atlas can show a live curve in a browser at all. A 128×128 lattice has 32 512 open-boundary edges; a Newman–Ziff sweep over that lattice is a few million DSU operations, which is well inside a frame budget when the sweep is chunked. The laboratories use the same code path as the libraries; there is no separate "demo" implementation to drift out of sync.

entries.chapterTitle: Directed percolation: time as a direction
entries.heading: Directed percolation: time as a direction
entries.text: Ordinary percolation has no arrow of time. A path may wander left, right, backwards or forwards, and the only constraint is connectivity. Directed percolation adds a direction: an open edge may be traversed in one sense only. The change looks minor and is not. It removes loops, changes the universality class, and produces the most robust universality class in non-equilibrium statistical physics.

entries.chapterTitle: Directed percolation: time as a direction
entries.heading: 16.1 The model
entries.text: Work on {Z}^d {Z} { 0}. For each site x and each of the d positive coordinate directions e i, declare the directed edge (x,t) (x+e i,t+1) open with probability p, independently. A directed path is a sequence of open edges with increasing time. The directed cluster of (x,t) is the set of sites reachable from it. The order parameter is For d=1 the lattice is a tilted square lattice: one spatial direction and one time direction, usually written 1+1. For d=2 it is 2+1. The interactive laboratory uses the 1+1 case: east edges are space, south edges are time. The first structural difference from ordinary percolation is that a directed cluster cannot close a loop in time. A directed path that returns to the same time slice would need a backward edge, and there are none. This is why the branching approximation is quantitatively useful in a way that it is not for the undirected lattice: the genealogical tree of a directed cluster has no cycles to correct.

entries.chapterTitle: Directed percolation: time as a direction
entries.heading: 16.2 Mean field, done exactly
entries.text: On a directed tree with d forward branches per site, let r be the probability that a site reached at time t has an infinite forward cluster. Its d children are independent, each is reached with probability p, and each then has an infinite forward cluster with probability r. Hence The trivial solution r=0 always exists. A positive solution appears when the right-hand side has slope greater than one at r=0: For p=p c(1+ ), expand r to second order. With s=pr, so, using dp=1+ , Thus =1 in mean field. The spatial correlation length is the distance over which the branching process forgets its starting point; a random walk with d choices has diffusive spread, so ^{-1/2} and =1/2. The temporal correlation length counts generations, so ^{-1} and =1. The dynamic exponent is z= / =2. The upper critical dimension is d c=4 spatial dimensions; above it these mean-field values are exact, with logarithmic corrections at d=4.

entries.chapterTitle: Directed percolation: time as a direction
entries.heading: 16.3 The exponents
entries.text: Write At criticality the survival probability decays as because a cluster that survives to time t has probability t^{- / } to be connected to the origin. The relation is a scaling identity, not an independent exponent. Class z status --- --- --- --- --- --- Mean field (d 4) 1 1/2 1 2 exact 1+1 0.276486(8) 1.096854(4) 1.733847(6) 1.5807 numerical 2+1 0.5836(6) 0.7329(6) 1.2950(5) 1.767 numerical The 1+1 values are known to about seven digits from long Monte Carlo runs and series extrapolations; the 2+1 values are known to three or four. Neither is a theorem. The table is included because the contrast with ordinary percolation is the point: 0.276 is not 5/36 0.139, and the two transitions are in different universality classes even though both live on a square lattice.

entries.chapterTitle: Directed percolation: time as a direction
entries.heading: 16.4 The DP conjecture
entries.text: The reason directed percolation matters beyond its own lattice is a conjecture, not a theorem. Conjecture 16.1 (Janssen 1981; Grassberger 1982). Consider a continuous phase transition from an absorbing state to an active state in a system with a scalar order parameter, short-range interactions, no additional conservation law and no quenched disorder. Then the transition belongs to the directed-percolation universality class. The conditions are the content. A conserved density, a second absorbing state, long-range interactions, quenched randomness or a coupling to a conserved field can change the class. The contact process, the Schlögl second model and a number of reaction-diffusion systems satisfy the conditions and reproduce DP exponents. The experimental confirmation in turbulent liquid crystals (Takeuchi et al. 2007) is the cleanest physical instance. The conjecture is not proved in general, and it is not a licence to call every absorbing-state transition DP. It is a checklist: identify the absorbing state, check that the order parameter is scalar, check that no conservation law survives, and check that the disorder is not quenched. A model that fails one item may still be in the class, but the burden of evidence is then on the model.

entries.chapterTitle: Directed percolation: time as a direction
entries.heading: 16.5 Simulation
entries.text: Directed reachability is cheaper than undirected connectivity because the time direction gives a topological order. On an L L square with east and south edges, process the sites in row-major order. A site is reachable if it is occupied (site mode), or if the edge from its west or north neighbour is open and that neighbour is reachable (bond mode). The left column is the source. A left-right crossing exists if any site in the last column is reachable. The dynamic program is O(L^2) after the configuration is drawn, and it uses O(L^2) memory for the reachable set. It consumes n uniforms in site mode and m in bond mode, in the same order as the undirected sampler, which is why the four libraries can share a parity probe. The reference values for the 1+1 square lattice are p c=0.644700(10) for bond and p c=0.705489(4) for site. Finite-size scaling works as in the undirected case, with one important difference: there is no duality identity that fixes the crossing probability at p c to 1/2. The crossing probability at p c approaches a universal constant that is not 1/2, and the approach is slow. A code calibrated only on the undirected square-lattice identity will therefore give a biased directed threshold. Use the collapse, not the level crossing.

entries.chapterTitle: Directed percolation: time as a direction
entries.heading: 16.6 Where the direction comes from
entries.text: Directed percolation is the natural model when the order of events matters. - Epidemics on temporal networks. A transmission path must respect time: an individual infected at time t can only infect a contact who is available after t. The static-network giant component is the wrong object; the temporal reachability graph is directed. - Forest fires and invasions. A fire spreading with a prevailing wind, or a species advancing into new territory, has a preferred direction. The front is a directed interface, and its roughness is a DP observable. - Directed polymers in random media. A path through a random environment with a preferred direction maps to a directed-walk problem; the free-energy fluctuations are governed by the Kardashev–Parisi–Zhang class, and the connection to DP is through the same directed geometry, not through an identity of exponents. - Absorbing-state dynamics. The contact process, catalytic reactions and Schlögl-type models sit in the DP class under the conditions of Conjecture 16.1. This is the largest application: DP is the default critical behaviour of a whole family of non-equilibrium systems. The unity is real but conditional. A model with a conservation law, a symmetry or a second absorbing state is not automatically DP, and the DP exponents should not be quoted for it without a check.

entries.chapterTitle: Directed percolation: time as a direction
entries.heading: 16.7 What the laboratory shows
entries.text: The directed laboratory draws a 1+1 bond or site configuration at full resolution, marks the reachable set, and reports the left-right crossing indicator. The controls are the same as in the undirected lattice laboratory, so the two can be compared directly: at the same p, the directed model is far below its threshold when the undirected model is already critical. The laboratory does not measure the exponent table. It shows the geometry that makes the exponents plausible: a directed cluster is a tree-like object with a well-defined front, and the front broadens as p approaches p c. The numerical values in the table come from the literature, not from the browser.

entries.chapterTitle: Continuum percolation: disks, rods, and real media
entries.heading: Continuum percolation: disks, rods, and real media
entries.text: Lattice percolation puts the randomness on a fixed grid. A composite, a sensor field or a porous rock does not have a grid: the filler particles sit at random positions, and two particles are connected when their excluded volumes overlap. The continuum version of the model is the Boolean model, and its threshold is a number that every application quotes and few applications check.

entries.chapterTitle: Continuum percolation: disks, rods, and real media
entries.heading: 17.1 The Boolean model
entries.text: Let the centres of the particles be a Poisson point process of intensity n in the plane, and let each particle be a closed disk of radius r. Two disks are connected when they overlap or touch, i.e. when the distance between their centres is at most 2r. The connected components of this intersection graph are the continuum clusters. The natural dimensionless control parameter is the reduced density the expected number of disk centres in a disk of radius r. It is the continuum analogue of np. The model is scale-free in the sense that only matters, not n and r separately, as long as the domain is large compared with r.

entries.chapterTitle: Continuum percolation: disks, rods, and real media
entries.heading: 17.2 Coverage is smooth
entries.text: Fix a point x. The number of centres in the disk of radius r around x is Poisson with mean , so This is the expected covered area fraction, and it is a smooth function of with no threshold. The derivative e^{- } is largest at =0 and decreases monotonically; there is no critical point in the coverage curve. The distinction matters because coverage and connectivity are routinely conflated in deployment calculations. A sensor field can cover 99% of a region and still fail to connect its two ends; a composite can be electrically connected at a filler fraction far below the fraction that covers the sample. Coverage is a statement about the union of disks. Connectivity is a statement about a spanning cluster in the intersection graph.

entries.chapterTitle: Continuum percolation: disks, rods, and real media
entries.heading: 17.3 The connectivity threshold
entries.text: The Boolean model has a percolation transition at a critical reduced density with the area fraction at the transition The value is numerical, not exact; the best estimates come from large-scale simulations and finite-size scaling (Mertens and Moore 2012). The threshold is for the infinite plane; a finite box has a rounded transition and a pseudocritical point that depends on the boundary conditions. A useful sanity check is the mean degree. A disk has, on average, neighbours, because the centre of a neighbouring disk must lie in a disk of radius 2r. At c this gives k 4.51. The number is not a threshold criterion — the degree distribution is Poisson and the clustering is geometric — but it is a quick check that a simulation is in the right range. A code that reports a threshold at k 2 is describing a different graph.

entries.chapterTitle: Continuum percolation: disks, rods, and real media
entries.heading: 17.4 Excluded volume and anisotropic fillers
entries.text: The disk model is isotropic. Real fillers are rods, plates and irregular particles, and their shape changes the threshold by orders of magnitude. The organising quantity is the excluded volume V {ex}: the volume swept by one particle around another when the two are in contact. For two convex bodies of volume v, the percolation threshold scales as up to a shape-dependent prefactor of order one. The relation is not exact, but it explains the scaling that matters. For a thin rod of length L and diameter D, v L D^2 and V {ex} L^2D, so For a thin plate of diameter L and thickness D, the same dimensional argument gives c D/L. This is why carbon nanotubes and graphene percolate at fractions one or two orders of magnitude below spherical carbon black: the aspect ratio L/D multiplies the excluded volume without multiplying the mass. The excluded-volume argument assumes hard, randomly oriented, well-dispersed particles. Agglomeration reduces the effective aspect ratio and raises the threshold; alignment changes the threshold in a direction-dependent way, so a single scalar c is no longer the right object. The correct object is a directional threshold tensor, and the engineering target is a formulation that sits above the threshold in every direction that carries current or load.

entries.chapterTitle: Continuum percolation: disks, rods, and real media
entries.heading: 17.5 Simulation
entries.text: The direct algorithm is the same as the lattice one, with geometry replacing the edge list. Generate n Poisson points in the box. Bucket them into a uniform grid with cell size 2r. For each disk, inspect the nine neighbouring cells and union the disks whose centres are within 2r. The expected work is O(n) when the density is moderate, because the number of neighbours per cell is bounded by the Poisson mean. Two corrections are easy to miss. First, the grid must cover the box with a halo of one cell, or pairs that straddle a boundary are lost. Second, the finite box has a boundary layer of width 2r in which clusters are truncated; the largest-cluster fraction should be measured in the interior or the boundary conditions should be stated. The laboratory uses periodic images for the neighbour search but reports the largest cluster in the fundamental box, which is a compromise: it removes the worst boundary bias without pretending that a small box is infinite.

entries.chapterTitle: Continuum percolation: disks, rods, and real media
entries.heading: 17.6 Applications
entries.text: Sensor networks. Coverage asks whether every point is within range of some sensor; connectivity asks whether the communication graph has a spanning component. The two thresholds differ, and a deployment that satisfies one may fail the other. The Boolean model gives the scaling law; the actual radio range, obstacles and sleep schedules are corrections that must be measured. Conductive composites. The filler network is a continuum percolation problem with tunnelling. The threshold is set by the excluded volume and the dispersion; the conductivity above it is set by the contact resistance and the tunnelling barriers. Percolation predicts where the jump occurs, not how large it is. Porous media. The pore space is the connected phase; the solid matrix is the obstacle. Mercury intrusion, drainage and imbibition are invasion problems with a threshold set by the throat-size distribution. The Boolean model is a crude geometry for the pore space, but it captures the difference between a connected and a disconnected pore network. Tissue scaffolds. Cells migrate through connected pores. The scaffold must be above the pore-connectivity threshold, not merely porous. The threshold depends on the pore-size distribution relative to the cell size, which makes it a weighted percolation problem rather than a Boolean one.

entries.chapterTitle: Continuum percolation: disks, rods, and real media
entries.heading: 17.7 What the Boolean model does not capture
entries.text: The model assumes hard impenetrable disks, a Poisson distribution of centres, no orientational correlations and no contacts beyond geometric overlap. Real systems violate every assumption to some degree. Polydispersity broadens the transition; clustering creates dense regions and voids; alignment makes the threshold anisotropic; tunnelling and contact resistance add a transport layer that percolation does not describe. The right response is not to abandon the model but to use it for what it does well: the scaling of the threshold with aspect ratio, the distinction between coverage and connectivity, and the order of magnitude of the critical fraction. The prefactor and the amplitude require a more detailed model, and the measurement should be designed to test the scaling rather than to confirm a single number.

entries.chapterTitle: Continuum percolation: disks, rods, and real media
entries.heading: 17.8 Open questions
entries.text: The exact c of the Poisson disk model is not known. The value is known numerically to several digits, and the universality class is the same as lattice percolation in two dimensions, but a proof is missing. The same is true for the threshold of anisotropic particles, polydisperse mixtures and systems with attractive interactions. These are not exotic questions: they are the questions that decide whether a composite formulation or a sensor deployment will work.

entries.heading: Transport and first passage
entries.text: Connectivity answers a yes/no question: is there a path? Transport asks how much, how fast, and how variable. The two are related but not interchangeable. A cluster can be connected and still conduct poorly, and a connected network can have arrival times so heavy-tailed that the mean is not a useful summary. This chapter gives the exponents and the measurement protocol that separate the two.

entries.heading: 18.1 Conductivity
entries.text: Put a unit voltage across a percolation cluster and measure the current. Near p c the effective conductivity vanishes as The exponent t is not the conductivity of a single bond; it is the macroscopic response of a fractal network with dangling ends, bottlenecks and loops. The standard scaling relation is where is the resistance exponent, the anomalous dimension that measures how resistance grows with Euclidean distance on the cluster. In two dimensions t 1.299 (Grassberger 1999); in three dimensions t 2.0. Neither is known exactly in three dimensions. The two-dimensional value is numerical, not a conformal-field-theory theorem, and it should be quoted with its uncertainty. The naive Einstein relation identifies conductivity with a diffusion coefficient. It fails at p c because the random walk on the cluster is anomalous: the mean-square displacement grows as with a walk dimension d w larger than the diffusive value two. The spectral dimension controls the return probability and the low-frequency density of states. In two dimensions d w 2.878 and d s 1.318; in three dimensions d w 3.88 and d s 1.30. The numbers are numerical; the relation d s=2d f/d w is a definition plus the fractal geometry, not an independent theorem.

entries.heading: 18.2 Why the exponents differ
entries.text: Three geometric features separate transport from connectivity. - Dangling ends. A large fraction of the cluster mass hangs from the conducting backbone and carries no current. The backbone is thinner than the cluster, so the conductivity is lower than a naive counting of sites would suggest. - Bottlenecks. Current must pass through narrow necks. The resistance is dominated by the narrowest cuts, not by the average width. - Loops. A loop gives an alternative path and lowers the resistance, but it also adds a length scale that the walk must explore. The competition between loops and bottlenecks is what makes nontrivial. The same three features explain why the diffusion coefficient and the conductivity are not proportional. A walker spends most of its time in dangling ends, which carry no current; the current uses the backbone, which the walker visits rarely. The Einstein relation is restored only if the walk is averaged over the same measure as the current, which is not the simple site measure.

entries.heading: 18.3 First passage
entries.text: The first-passage time from a source to a target is the random time at which a walker first reaches the target. On a percolation cluster near p c, its distribution is broad. The mean is dominated by rare slow paths and is often a poor summary; quantiles and the full distribution are more informative. For a one-dimensional chain the first-passage density decays as t^{-3/2} for large t, a universal tail that follows from the central limit theorem for the underlying random walk. On a fractal the tail is modified by the walk dimension and the spectral dimension. The practical consequence is the same: near the threshold, a small fraction of trajectories takes a very long time, and a risk calculation based on the mean arrival time underestimates the tail. This is not a mathematical curiosity. Contaminant transport in a heterogeneous aquifer, message delivery in a delay-tolerant network, and the search time of a foraging animal all show heavy-tailed first-passage distributions near a connectivity threshold. The correct engineering question is usually a quantile — "what is the 95th percentile arrival time?" — not the mean.

entries.heading: 18.4 Algorithms
entries.text: Three computations cover most of the applications. Shortest path. On an unweighted graph, breadth-first search from the source gives the graph distance to every vertex in O(n+m). On a weighted graph, Dijkstra's algorithm with a binary heap costs O((n+m) n). The shortest path is not the first-passage path of a random walk, but it is the right object for routing and for the "best case" arrival time. Conductivity. Solve the Laplacian linear system with a unit voltage on the source and sink. The effective conductance is the current. Direct solvers cost O(n^3) in the worst case; sparse Cholesky, multigrid or a conjugate-gradient method with a good preconditioner brings large two- and three-dimensional systems into range. The atlas does not ship a Laplacian solver; the exponent table is quoted from the literature, and a production calculation needs a dedicated numerical library. Random walk. Simulate many independent walkers, record the first-passage time to the target, and report the empirical distribution and its quantiles. The cost is O( {walkers} {steps}); the variance of the tail estimate is controlled by the number of walkers that actually reach the target, not by the total number of steps.

entries.heading: 18.5 Applications
entries.text: Composite conductivity. The percolation threshold sets where the conductivity jump occurs; the exponent t sets how steep it is; the contact resistance sets the amplitude. A formulation that is barely above the threshold is sensitive to batch-to-batch variation, because the slope is largest there. Porous media. The relative permeability curve is a transport observable, not a connectivity observable. Near the irreducible saturation the water phase is connected but poorly conducting; the exponent and the bottleneck geometry determine the shape of the curve. Epidemics and networks. The arrival time of an epidemic or a message is a first-passage observable. The giant component tells you whether arrival is possible; the tail tells you how long it may take. The two questions need different models. Sensor and infrastructure networks. Connectivity is necessary for operation but not sufficient for performance. Latency, capacity and failure propagation are transport questions, and a network that is connected can still be unusable under load.

entries.heading: 18.6 What to report
entries.text: A transport measurement should report the exponent, the interval over which it was fitted, the geometry (backbone or full cluster), the boundary conditions, and the uncertainty. It should also report the first-passage quantiles if the application cares about time. A single conductivity number at one volume fraction is not a percolation result; it is one point on a curve whose shape is the actual prediction. The distinction between connectivity and transport is the last piece of the atlas's recurring theme. Percolation gives the threshold and the scaling with remarkable reliability. It gives amplitudes and dynamics poorly or not at all. An application that respects the division of labour is useful; one that quotes a threshold as a material constant is not.

entries.chapterTitle: Proofs, algorithms and the status of a claim
entries.heading: Proofs, algorithms and the status of a claim
entries.text: This atlas mixes three kinds of statement: theorems with complete proofs, theorems whose proofs are too long to reproduce but whose hypotheses and conclusions are stated, and numerical observations. Conflating them is the most common way a percolation argument goes wrong. This appendix states the main results, gives the short proofs, sketches the long ones, and gives the correctness argument for every algorithm in the reference library.

entries.chapterTitle: Proofs, algorithms and the status of a claim
entries.heading: 19.1 A status vocabulary
entries.text: Every claim in the atlas carries one of four labels. - Theorem. A proven statement. The proof is either written out here or cited to a specific theorem in a specific source. - Proof sketch. The mechanism is correct and the missing step is a standard compactness, coupling or finite-volume argument. A sketch is not a substitute for a proof in a paper submission. - Numerical. A value produced by a finite simulation with a stated seed, size and criterion. It is reproducible, not exact. - Conjecture. A statement with strong evidence and no proof. Conjectures are labelled in the text, not quietly promoted. The distinction matters because percolation has a large literature of exact thresholds, and a reader who cannot tell an exact value from an extrapolation will overstate the precision of an applied model.

entries.chapterTitle: Proofs, algorithms and the status of a claim
entries.heading: 19.2 Positive association: Harris and FKG
entries.text: Let =\{0,1\}^{E} with the product measure {P} p, and order configurations by inclusion. An event is increasing if adding open edges cannot destroy it; examples are “there is a left–right crossing” and “ C(0) k”. Theorem (Harris 1960; FKG 1971). If A and B are increasing, then Proof sketch. Couple two configurations ' by the same uniforms: declare e open in if U e p and in ' if U e q, with p q. This monotone coupling preserves the order. A pointwise inequality for monotone set functions on the Boolean lattice (the four-function argument of Harris, or the lattice argument of Fortuin–Kasteleyn–Ginibre) then gives the result. The key point is that the inequality is a statement about the measure, not about a particular graph. Two consequences are used repeatedly. First, the probability of a crossing is increasing in p, so the critical point is well defined as a supremum. Second, if A is increasing and B is decreasing, the inequality reverses. Harris's original application was a lower bound for p c on the square lattice. FKG turned the idea into a general tool for ferromagnetic systems.

entries.chapterTitle: Proofs, algorithms and the status of a claim
entries.heading: 19.3 Disjoint occurrence: the BK inequality
entries.text: FKG compares events that may overlap. The BK inequality compares events that must occur on disjoint edge sets. For increasing events A and B, let A B be the event that there are disjoint sets of open edges witnessing A and B. Then (van den Berg and Kesten 1985). This is not true for general measures; it is a property of product measures and of the models obtained from them by the usual coupling arguments. The standard use is the tail of the cluster size. If \{ C(0) n\} occurs, one can split the cluster at a suitable edge into two disjoint crossing events; BK converts the resulting recursive bound into exponential decay for p

entries.chapterTitle: Proofs, algorithms and the status of a claim
entries.heading: 19.4 Uniqueness of the infinite cluster
entries.text: Theorem (Burton and Keane 1989). For Bernoulli percolation on an amenable transitive graph such as {Z}^d, there is at most one infinite cluster almost surely, for every p. Proof sketch. Suppose two infinite clusters were disjoint with positive probability. By finite energy, one can flip a finite set of edges to merge them without changing the probability by more than a constant factor. A local modification argument then shows that the number of infinite clusters cannot be a non-constant finite random variable, and an amenability argument rules out infinitely many. The complete argument is short but not trivial. The conclusion is false on a regular tree, where infinitely many infinite clusters coexist for a range of p: amenability is doing real work. Uniqueness is what lets one speak of “the” infinite cluster and of the percolation probability (p)= {P} p(0 ) without ambiguity.

entries.chapterTitle: Proofs, algorithms and the status of a claim
entries.heading: 19.5 Duality and exact thresholds
entries.text: On the square lattice, the dual of a bond configuration is another bond configuration on the shifted lattice: an edge is open in the dual exactly when the primal edge is closed. For a box n, a left–right open crossing of n exists iff there is no top–bottom closed crossing of the matching box n^ . This gives the finite-box identity At p=1/2 colour symmetry makes B n^ an open top–bottom crossing of the dual box. The dual box does not have the same vertex count as n, so the two probabilities are not equal at finite n; their difference is a boundary term. Taking n and using Proposition 4.3 gives {P} {1/2}(A n) 1/2. Harris used this limiting statement to prove p c 1/2; Kesten (1980) proved p c 1/2 by a more delicate argument, so p c=1/2 exactly. At finite n the crossing probability is not 1/2: exact enumeration gives 3/4, 43/64 and 82623/131072 on the 2 2, 3 3 and 4 4 vertex boxes. The triangular and honeycomb thresholds follow from the star–triangle transformation. The bond thresholds are and the square value is 1/2 (Sykes and Essam 1964; Wierman 1981). These are exact, not fits. No such identity is known for site percolation on the square lattice; the numerical value 0.592746 is not a closed form. The directed model has no duality at p c, which is why its crossing probability at threshold is not 1/2.

entries.chapterTitle: Proofs, algorithms and the status of a claim
entries.heading: 19.6 Sharpness, RSW and the critical window
entries.text: Duality gives the threshold on special lattices; it does not show that the transition is sharp on a general graph. The modern route has three steps. 1. RSW. For Bernoulli percolation on the square lattice, crossing probabilities of rectangles are bounded above and below uniformly in the aspect ratio, at p=1/2 (Russo 1978; Seymour and Welsh 1978). 2. Sharpness. Aizenman and Barsky (1987) and Menshikov (1986) proved that for p

entries.chapterTitle: Proofs, algorithms and the status of a claim
entries.heading: 19.7 Mean field and high dimensions
entries.text: Above the upper critical dimension d c=6, the critical exponents are expected to take their mean-field values with logarithmic corrections at d=6. Hara and Slade (1990) proved mean-field behaviour for sufficiently large d using the lace expansion; Fitzner and van der Hofstad (2017) extended the proof to all d 10. The case 7 d 10 and the logarithmic corrections at d=6 are active research areas, not settled textbook material. On a tree or a Bethe lattice the calculation is exact: the threshold is p c=1/(z-1) for degree z, and the exponents are mean-field. The tree is a useful check on any approximation, but it is not a model of a two-dimensional material.

entries.chapterTitle: Proofs, algorithms and the status of a claim
entries.heading: 19.8 Two-dimensional conformal invariance
entries.text: Cardy's formula (1992) gives the left–right crossing probability of a critical rectangle with wired left and right sides: where C is a normalisation constant and K is the complete elliptic integral. At =1, m=1/2 and =1/2. Smirnov (2001) proved conformal invariance for site percolation on the triangular lattice, which identifies the scaling limit with SLE 6; Lawler, Schramm and Werner computed the exponent values that follow. The formula is exact in the scaling limit. On a finite square lattice the measured crossing probability approaches it with a correction that vanishes as L grows; the laboratory shows both the curve and the measured points rather than hiding the correction.

entries.chapterTitle: Proofs, algorithms and the status of a claim
entries.heading: 19.9 Correctness of the algorithms
entries.text: The following statements are what the test suite checks; each is a small proof. Union–find. Invariant: find(x) returns the root of the tree containing x, and size[root] is the number of elements in that tree. Union by size attaches the smaller root under the larger, so a root of size s can only be attached to a root of size at least s; the depth is O( n). Path halving makes every other node on the path point to its grandparent, which gives the inverse-Ackermann amortised bound when combined with union by size (Tarjan 1975). Hoshen–Kopelman. Every site is visited once, and every edge between a site and an already visited neighbour is processed once. Two labels are unioned exactly when the corresponding components are connected by an open edge, so after the scan the label classes are the connected components. The scan is a spanning-forest construction, not an approximation. Newman–Ziff. After the first k edges of a uniform random permutation have been added, the open set is a sample from bond percolation at p=k/m. This is exact because a uniform permutation conditioned on its first k elements gives a uniform k-subset. The maintained second moment satisfies M 2 M 2+2ab when components of sizes a and b merge, so the reported susceptibility is exact for the sampled configuration, not an estimator of a different quantity. Leath growth. Conditional on the seed being occupied, every edge incident to a visited site is tested once with the correct Bernoulli probability. An open edge to an unvisited site is explored; a closed edge is recorded as perimeter. By induction on the BFS order, the visited set is exactly the cluster of the seed. The only bias is the optional size cutoff, which truncates the tail. Bootstrap closure. The update operator is monotone: if S T, then F(S) F(T). A monotone operator on a finite lattice has a least fixed point, obtained by iterating from the initial set. The queue algorithm activates a site at the first round at which its active-neighbour count reaches r, so it computes that least fixed point; ties and update order cannot change the result. Invasion percolation. The accepted edges form a tree: an edge is accepted only when it connects a visited site to an unvisited one, so no cycle is created, and every accepted site except the seed is reached by exactly one accepted edge. The greedy choice of the minimum boundary threshold is the definition of the process; the heap implements it exactly. The loop edges are discarded, not accepted. Achlioptas process. The DSU state after each step is the component partition of the graph containing the edges chosen so far. The rule selects one of two candidates using only the current component sizes, so the trajectory is a deterministic function of the candidate sequence and the initial graph. The finite-size jump in S { } is a property of that trajectory; it is not evidence of a thermodynamic discontinuity, and the scaling check in the laboratory is there to make the distinction visible.

entries.chapterTitle: Proofs, algorithms and the status of a claim
entries.heading: 19.10 Statistical error and finite-size bias
entries.text: A Monte Carlo estimate from n independent samples has standard error { (1- )/n}. A 95% interval is 1.96\, {se} for large n; for small n use a Wilson or Jeffreys interval, not the normal approximation. Hoeffding's inequality gives the distribution-free bound which is useful when a guaranteed accuracy is needed. Finite-size bias is a separate error. The crossing probability at p c converges to 1/2 only after a correction of order L^{-1/ }; the pseudo-critical point extracted from the susceptibility peak is shifted by a term of the same order. A fit that ignores the correction will report an exponent that depends on the range of L used. The correct protocol is to fit with a correction term, report the range, and show the residuals.

entries.chapterTitle: Proofs, algorithms and the status of a claim
entries.heading: 19.11 What is not known
entries.text: - The exact site-percolation threshold of the square lattice is not known in closed form. - The exact bond threshold in three dimensions is not known; the best numerical values have many digits but no proof. - The critical exponents in three dimensions are not proven to take any particular rational values. - The scaling limit of critical percolation in three dimensions is not constructed. - The sharpness of the transition for all transitive graphs is not known in full generality. Listing these is not a disclaimer; it is part of using the theory honestly. A numerical value in this atlas is never presented as a theorem, and a theorem is never presented without its hypotheses.

entries.chapterTitle: Proofs, algorithms and the status of a claim
entries.heading: 19.12 Reading the sources
entries.text: The primary sources for this appendix are Grimmett's Percolation (1999) for the rigorous core, Bollobás and Riordan's Percolation (2006) for the modern probabilistic treatment, and the original papers cited above. The proofs in this chapter are sketches where the full argument would run to several pages; they are labelled as sketches. The algorithms are checked by executable tests, not by the prose: see tests/js/algorithms.test.js, lib/python/tests/test algorithms.py and data/golden/algorithms-v3.json. A short shelf If you want one rigorous book, take Grimmett's Percolation ; if you want the modern probabilistic viewpoint with the proofs written for a graduate course, take Bollobás and Riordan. Stauffer and Aharony remains the quickest route into the physicists' language of exponents, and Sahimi's Applications of Percolation Theory is the bridge to porous media, composites and transport. Meester and Roy are the standard reference for continuum percolation; Hunt, Ewing and Ghanbarian go carefully from percolation to flow in real porous media. For networks, Newman's Networks is the general text, Dorogovtsev's Lectures on Complex Networks the compact theoretical one, and Bianconi's Multilayer Networks the right starting point when one layer is not enough. Lyons and Peres is the rigorous reference for trees and branching processes; Kiss, Miller and Simon, and Keeling and Rohani, are the right next step for epidemics. Christensen and Moloney connect percolation to criticality without hiding the physics. Bunde and Havlin, Hughes, and Zallen are older books that still repay reading: they contain the arguments and the experimental context that modern reviews compress away. Among reviews, Saberi (2015) and Li et al. (2021) are broad and well referenced; D'Souza et al. (2019) is the honest account of explosive percolation; Boccaletti et al. (2014) and Kivelä et al. (2014) cover multilayer networks from structure to dynamics. Isichenko (1992) is still the best long essay on percolation, statistical topography and transport in random media, and Berkowitz and Ewing (1998) is a compact introduction to the soil-physics applications. These are reading suggestions, not a canonical list. The bibliography in the Sources view is the complete record, with a DOI or URL for every entry and a note where a DOI does not exist.

entries.heading: Design under uncertainty
entries.text: The previous chapters answer “what happens at this density?”. Design asks the inverse question: “which density, which edges, which allocation gives a required reliability at acceptable cost?”. That inversion changes the mathematics. A percolation threshold becomes a constraint, a power-law becomes a cost curve, and a finite-size correction becomes the difference between a safe design and a failed one.

entries.heading: 20.1 The design template
entries.text: Every design problem in this chapter fits one template. 1. Decision variables. Which edges to add (x e \{0,1\}), which vertices to protect (y v), the filler fraction , the firebreak density , the number of sensors n, the coupling strength between layers. 2. Random medium. The realisation of open/closed elements, contact transmission, pore-size disorder or fuel connectivity. Its law is a model choice, and the model choice is part of the claim. 3. Performance functional. The probability of a spanning cluster, the size of the giant component, the expected fraction of demand served, the probability that a cascade stays below a budget, or a quantile of the first-passage time. 4. Cost. Money, mass, energy, added edges, vaccinated-person-days, maintenance. Design without a cost is a wish. 5. Constraint. A minimum reliability, a maximum budget, an equity constraint, or a regulatory limit. The output is not a single number but a curve: reliability versus cost. A design point is a point on that curve, and the curve is the useful object.

entries.heading: 20.2 Monotonicity is not submodularity
entries.text: Adding edges cannot reduce connectivity, so the performance functional is monotone in the set of edges. Monotonicity alone does not give a good greedy algorithm. The greedy guarantee for maximising a monotone submodular function requires diminishing returns: adding an edge to a small set must help at least as much as adding it to a large set. For coverage problems (union of disks, influence maximisation with independent cascade) submodularity holds and the greedy algorithm has a (1-1/e) guarantee. For connectivity the situation is different: adding an edge can be redundant in a large set and decisive in a small one, and the expected giant-component size is not generally submodular. Two honest options are available. - Use a surrogate that is submodular (coverage, spectral connectivity, number of protected demand pairs) and validate the final design with the true percolation objective. - Use a derivative-free or mixed-integer search with a stated optimality gap, and report that gap. Do not call a greedy heuristic optimal because the objective is monotone.

entries.heading: 20.3 Networks: robustness at a price
entries.text: The configuration-model result f c=1-1/( -1) with = k^2 / k says that heterogeneity protects against random loss and exposes the network to targeted loss. Design follows from the two terms. - Truncate the tail. Capping the degree at k { } reduces and makes the network less fragile under targeting, at the cost of the capacity that the hubs provided. The optimal cap is a cost problem, not a theorem. - Add redundancy, not just edges. A second path between two regions costs more than one extra edge but changes the failure mode from disconnection to graceful degradation. - Protect the hubs. Guarding a small number of high-degree vertices is efficient against targeted attack; it is almost useless against random loss. Allocate the budget according to the threat model, not according to the average degree. - Measure the right curve. A robustness audit that reports f c alone hides the cascade. Report S(f) for both random and targeted removal, with the number of cascade rounds. For coupled infrastructures the design variables are coupling strength and redundancy. A one-to-one dependency produces a first-order transition at p c=2.4554/c; partial coupling or multiple dependencies restores a continuous transition (Buldyrev et al. 2010; Parshani et al. 2010). The engineering question is not “is coupling bad?” but “how much coupling can we afford to remove?”.

entries.heading: 20.4 Epidemics: doses, targets and timing
entries.text: For an SIR process on a configuration-model network, the final size is the giant component after each edge is retained with the per-contact transmission probability T. With R 0=T( -1), random immunisation needs a fraction of the population. Targeted immunisation of high-degree vertices is more efficient when the degree distribution is heavy-tailed; the gain is largest exactly where random allocation is worst. Three design cautions. First, the formula is for a static network and a Markovian epidemic; temporal and behavioural networks change the threshold. Second, the herd-immunity threshold is about the final size in an infinite population, not the peak or the time course. Third, equity is a constraint, not an afterthought: the cheapest allocation by doses may systematically leave the most exposed group below its local threshold.

entries.heading: 20.5 Materials and electrodes: a narrow window
entries.text: A conductive composite needs the filler network above its percolation threshold. The threshold is controlled by geometry more than by mass: the excluded volume of a rod scales with its aspect ratio, so nanotubes and graphene percolate at fractions far below carbon black. The design variables are aspect ratio, dispersion quality, alignment and loading. The engineering optimum sits just above the threshold, where conductivity rises steeply with loading but the additive still displaces active material. That window is narrow for two reasons: the percolation conductivity is a power law, and the batch-to-batch scatter of the effective occupancy is largest near the threshold. A design that targets the middle of the window will fail on the low side of a batch distribution; a design that targets the upper edge pays an energy-density penalty. The robust choice depends on the cost of failure, not on the mean. The same structure appears in battery electrodes, fuel-cell catalyst layers, solid electrolytes and thermal interface materials: two or more networks must percolate simultaneously, which is a two-phase percolation problem, not two independent ones.

entries.heading: 20.6 Porous media and energy storage
entries.text: In a porous rock the pore space is the site graph and the throats are the bonds. The water-filled subgraph thins as saturation falls, and the hydraulic conductance vanishes at a critical saturation. The design variables are pore-size distribution, wettability and the fracture/matrix contrast. Invasion percolation is the right model when the displacement is controlled by the capillary pressure threshold, not by random occupation. The invasive cluster follows the lowest-threshold boundary edge, so the path is selected, not sampled. This is why a single “critical saturation” is not a material constant: it depends on the pressure path and on the ratio of throat sizes. For contaminant transport, the practical output is a quantile of the arrival-time distribution, not its mean; near the threshold the mean is dominated by rare fast paths.

entries.heading: 20.7 Fire, sensors, images and tissue
entries.text: Wildfire. Fuel connectivity is the control parameter. A firebreak reduces the effective density; the percolation picture says the change in fire size per unit of treatment is largest near the threshold, so a treatment density that is “almost enough” is the worst place to be. The design question is where to place the treatment, not only how much: a barrier that does not close a spanning path buys little. Sensor deployment. Coverage and connectivity are different functionals. Coverage is the area fraction of the union of disks, 1-e^{- } for a Poisson deployment; connectivity is a spanning cluster with onset c 1.128 in two dimensions (Mertens and Moore 2012). At 0.7 the field can be 50% covered and still disconnected. A deployment rule that equates the two overstates reliability. Image segmentation. Thresholding an image and taking the largest connected component is percolation on a correlated field. The choice of threshold is the choice of p. Hysteresis (a high threshold for seeds, a low threshold for growth) is a finite-size correction to a critical phenomenon; it works because the two thresholds separate the nucleation and the growth of the structure of interest. Tissue engineering. A scaffold must have connected pores above the cell-size cutoff. The relevant model is weighted percolation: a pore below the cell diameter is closed for migration even if it is geometrically open. The design variable is the pore-size distribution, not the mean porosity.

entries.heading: 20.8 A scenario table
entries.text: Domain Control variable Performance Main constraint Suggested method Validation --- --- --- --- --- --- Communication network added links, degree cap giant component under attack budget, latency multi-objective search + percolation audit targeted/random S(f) Epidemic vaccine doses, target group final size below budget doses, equity percolation threshold + allocation LP contact-network simulation Power/communication coupling coupling strength, redundancy cascade size cost, operating limits coupled giant-component iteration N-1 and N-k scenarios Conductive composite filler fraction, aspect ratio conductivity above target viscosity, cost excluded-volume estimate + percolation curve batch distribution Battery electrode additive loading, calendering rate capability energy density two-phase percolation window impedance + cycling Porous medium pore-size distribution, wettability hydraulic conductance permeability, cost invasion percolation / effective medium core-flood data Wildfire treatment placement, density fire size distribution budget, ecology percolation threshold + spatial optimisation landscape simulation Sensor field number, radius, placement coverage and connectivity cost, power Boolean model + connectivity audit deployment test Scaffold pore-size distribution connected pore fraction stiffness, manufacturability weighted percolation imaging + cell penetration The table is a map, not a recipe. Each row needs its own model validation; the percolation part supplies thresholds and scaling, not the amplitude.

entries.heading: 20.9 Optimisation algorithms, honestly
entries.text: Three families are useful. - Exact on small instances. Mixed-integer programming for edge selection with a connectivity cut, solved to a stated gap for graphs up to a few hundred edges. The percolation objective is replaced by a deterministic connectivity constraint on a scenario set; the result is only as good as the scenario set. - Greedy with a surrogate. Coverage, spectral connectivity or protected demand pairs are submodular or nearly so. Use the (1-1/e) guarantee for the surrogate, then re-evaluate on the true percolation objective. Report both numbers. - Stochastic search. Simulated annealing or evolutionary search on the edge set, with the percolation objective estimated by Monte Carlo. The noise in the objective is part of the algorithm; use common random numbers across candidate designs so that comparisons are not dominated by sampling noise. A design claimed to be optimal should state the objective, the scenario distribution, the solver, the gap or the number of samples, and the validation set. Without those, “optimal” means “the best point we happened to try”.

entries.heading: 20.10 Validation and the cost of being wrong
entries.text: A percolation design is a model-based decision, and the model has four error sources: the graph, the occupation law, the finite-size correction and the performance estimator. A validation protocol should address each. 1. Hold out a network or a batch. Fit on one realisation, test on another. A design that only works on the graph used to tune it is overfitted. 2. Report the finite-size gap. If the design is evaluated on L=64 but deployed at L=10^6, say so and estimate the direction of the bias. 3. Stress the tail. Evaluate at the 5th and 95th percentiles of the uncertain parameters, not only at the mean. 4. Compare with a trivial baseline. Random allocation, uniform loading, no treatment. A complex optimisation that beats the baseline by less than its own uncertainty is not evidence. 5. State the failure mode. Disconnection, cascade, slow drift, or a threshold that moves with temperature. The failure mode determines which metric matters. The honest summary is uncomfortable but useful: percolation is excellent at telling you where the cliff is and how steep it is, and poor at telling you the exact height of the fence you need. Design with the cliff in mind, measure the fence, and keep a margin for the part of the model you cannot verify.

entries.chapterTitle: Reproducibility, uncertainty and the error budget
entries.heading: Reproducibility, uncertainty and the error budget
entries.text: A result that cannot be reproduced is a story. This chapter states the contract the atlas uses, the commands that check it, and the places where a careful reader should still be suspicious. The goal is not to claim that every number is exact; it is to make every number traceable to a seed, a size, an estimator and a version.

entries.chapterTitle: Reproducibility, uncertainty and the error budget
entries.heading: 21.1 The artifact contract
entries.text: The repository is the artifact. Five things are versioned together. 1. Sources. Markdown chapters, JSON bibliography, citation map. 2. Engine. C++20, Julia, Python and JavaScript implementations of the Bernoulli core, the v3 algorithm zoo, the labelling routine and the tree/epidemic solvers. 3. Goldens. data/golden/parity.json for the four-language core, data/golden/rng-seed42.json for the random stream, data/golden/algorithms-v3.json for the new algorithms. 4. Data. Raw benchmark counts and the analysed record, with the harness that produced them. 5. Build and deploy. The content builder, the static server, the Python package, the API, the Dockerfile and the CI workflows. A change to the RNG, the edge order or the consumption order is a breaking change. It requires regenerating the goldens, bumping the version and recording the correction in Chapter 14. The same applies to a change in a sampling convention, even if the code still “looks right”.

entries.chapterTitle: Reproducibility, uncertainty and the error budget
entries.heading: 21.2 The random stream
entries.text: The generator is xoshiro128 with SplitMix32 seeding. The conventions are fixed: - the seed is reduced modulo 2^{32}; - seeding performs four SplitMix32 steps; - random() consumes two 32-bit outputs, high 26 bits then low 27 bits, and returns an exact multiple of 2^{-53} in [0,1); - int(n) uses rejection sampling against the largest multiple of n not exceeding 2^{32}; - site percolation draws n uniforms in site order; bond percolation draws m uniforms in the edge order produced by build lattice. Every implementation follows this order. The golden file stores raw outputs after a fixed number of draws, so a disagreement is caught before it becomes a wrong exponent. The full specification is in docs/RNG.md.

entries.chapterTitle: Reproducibility, uncertainty and the error budget
entries.heading: 21.3 The parity tests
entries.text: The core parity contract is four-language. scripts/parity.py computes the Python probes, runs scripts/parity probe.mjs for JavaScript, and compares both with data/golden/parity.json; the C++ and Julia suites assert the same values from the same file. The algorithm zoo has a four-language contract. scripts/parity algorithms.py compares Python and JavaScript on bootstrap activation times, invasion order, Leath cluster size and the Achlioptas trajectories; the C++ and Julia suites assert the same data/golden/algorithms-v3.json values, together with the deterministic Hoshen–Kopelman, Bethe and SIR probes. Run them with: A parity test is not a statistical test. It says that two implementations agree on an integer or an exact component size for a fixed input. That is the strongest check available before a statistical comparison, and it is the one that catches the majority of silent bugs.

entries.chapterTitle: Reproducibility, uncertainty and the error budget
entries.heading: 21.4 The statistical protocol
entries.text: A Monte Carlo estimate needs four numbers: the sample size, the seed (or the seed list), the estimator and the uncertainty. The atlas uses the following rules. - Independent seeds, not one long run. For a threshold estimate, run R independent seeds, each producing an estimate, and report the mean and the standard error over the R estimates. A single long run underestimates the variance because successive configurations are correlated. - Common random numbers for comparisons. When comparing two algorithms or two designs, use the same disorder realisations. The comparison is then paired, and the variance of the difference is much smaller than the variance of either mean. - Blocking for correlated sweeps. A Newman–Ziff sweep produces correlated points. Error bars come from independent edge orders, not from the m points along one order. - Intervals, not standard deviations. Report a 95% interval. For a proportion near 0 or 1 use Wilson or Jeffreys; for a small number of seeds use a t interval and say so. - Pre-register the stopping rule. “We ran until it looked converged” is not a stopping rule. Fix the number of seeds or the target half-width in advance.

entries.chapterTitle: Reproducibility, uncertainty and the error budget
entries.heading: 21.5 The error budget
entries.text: Every numerical claim in the atlas has an error budget with five lines. Source What it is How it is controlled Typical size --- --- --- --- Random stream finite sample of disorder independent seeds, paired comparisons O(n^{-1/2}) Finite size L/ not infinite collapse fit, correction term, several L O(L^{-1/ }) Discretisation lattice or time step approximates a continuum refine the step, compare two resolutions problem-specific Estimator bias e.g. S=0.5 crossing instead of a collapse use the better estimator, report both 10^{-2} in the teaching benchmark Model error the graph or occupation law is wrong validation on held-out data, sensitivity analysis often dominant The last line is the one that matters most in applications and the one that a simulation cannot reduce. A percolation model with a perfect error bar on the wrong graph is still wrong.

entries.chapterTitle: Reproducibility, uncertainty and the error budget
entries.heading: 21.6 Reproducing a figure
entries.text: Each figure in the Data view names its source record and the command that produced it. The sequence is: The benchmark is a teaching dataset, not a high-precision measurement. It is sized to run in minutes and to make finite-size behaviour visible. The Data view shows the exact sample sizes, the seed and the date; if the file is missing, it shows the commands instead of inventing a curve.

entries.chapterTitle: Reproducibility, uncertainty and the error budget
entries.heading: 21.7 The algorithm package
entries.text: The Python package is the distributable form of the engine. atlas-perc serve exposes the same static site plus a JSON API: Route Purpose --- --- GET /api/health version, build time, engine status GET /api/thresholds exact and numerical thresholds with status POST /api/sample one configuration, cluster statistics POST /api/sweep Newman–Ziff curve POST /api/bootstrap bootstrap closure POST /api/invasion invasion cluster POST /api/explosive Achlioptas trajectory GET /api/openapi.json machine-readable schema The API is intentionally small and has no authentication. It is a reference service, not a production multi-tenant deployment. For a public deployment, put it behind a rate limiter and a reverse proxy; the Dockerfile is a starting point, not a hardened appliance.

entries.chapterTitle: Reproducibility, uncertainty and the error budget
entries.heading: 21.8 A reporting checklist
entries.text: Before a percolation number leaves the notebook, answer these questions. - [ ] Is the model stated as a graph plus an occupation law? - [ ] Are the boundary conditions stated (open, periodic, wired)? - [ ] Is the estimator defined, and is it the one you actually computed? - [ ] Is the sample size given, and is the seed or seed list archived? - [ ] Is the uncertainty a standard error, a confidence interval or a standard deviation? - [ ] Is the finite-size correction estimated, or is the claim explicitly asymptotic? - [ ] Is the value labelled exact, numerical or conjectural? - [ ] Is the code version or commit recorded? - [ ] Does a second implementation reproduce the integer probes? - [ ] Is the failure mode of the model stated? A reader who can answer all ten can reproduce the number. A reader who cannot has a story, not a result.

entries.chapterTitle: Reproducibility, uncertainty and the error budget
entries.heading: 21.9 What cannot be reproduced
entries.text: Three things in this atlas are not bit-reproducible. 1. Wall-clock timings. The algorithm studio reports browser timings for teaching; they depend on the machine, the JIT and the load. Use the C++ harness for measurements intended to compare implementations. 2. Floating-point transcendental functions. sin, exp, log and the hypergeometric evaluation can differ in the last bits across libm versions. The golden files use tolerances for those values and exact equality only for integers and component sizes. 3. A published web page. The live site can change after a release. The repository tag and the archived site/ artifact are the reproducible objects; the URL is a convenience. Being explicit about these limits is part of the reproducibility claim, not a contradiction of it.

entries.chapterTitle: Trees, generating functions, and message passing
entries.heading: Trees, generating functions, and message passing
entries.text: Every exact calculation in this atlas that is not two-dimensional is a calculation on a tree. The Bethe lattice is the cleanest of them, but it is not the only one: a sparse random graph looks like a tree in the neighbourhood of a typical vertex, and the configuration model inherits the tree answer globally because its giant component is born by branching. This chapter derives the three equations that do most of the work — the branching recursion, the generating-function fixed point, and the message-passing system — and states precisely when each is exact and when it is only a local approximation.

entries.chapterTitle: Trees, generating functions, and message passing
entries.heading: 22.1 Bond percolation on a Galton–Watson tree
entries.text: Let T be a Galton–Watson tree: the root has K children with {P}(K=k)=p k, and every other vertex has an independent copy of the same offspring law. Write for the offspring generating function and its mean, and assume m 1 so that the tree is infinite with positive probability. Put bond percolation with retention probability p on the edges. Let u be the probability that the open cluster of a vertex, restricted to its descendant subtree , is finite. The vertex itself is present. Each child branch is finite if either the edge to that child is closed (probability 1-p) or it is open and the child's descendant cluster is finite (probability p\,u). The branches are independent given the vertex, so The root has the same offspring law, so its cluster is finite with probability u as well: The fixed point u=1 always solves (22.1) and gives =0. A second solution in [0,1) exists exactly when the map g(u)=f(1-p+pu) has slope greater than one at u=1: Hence This is the whole mean-field theory in three lines. For the z-regular tree the root has z neighbours and every other vertex has z-1 forward neighbours; the forward recursion is and p c=1/(z-1), the value quoted in Chapters 4 and 8. The two forms differ only in the root's degree; both are exact on their respective trees. For z=2 the tree is a chain: p c=1, and at p=1 the chain is fully open with =1. The endpoint is the one place where the "critical means =0" shorthand needs the obvious exception. Mean cluster size. The expected number of vertices at distance n from the root is m^n in the tree, and each is connected to the root with probability p^n. Hence which diverges as p p c=1/m with exponent =1. On the z-regular tree the count at distance n 1 is z(z-1)^{n-1}, so =1+zp/(1-p(z-1)); the divergence is the same.

entries.chapterTitle: Trees, generating functions, and message passing
entries.heading: 22.2 The cluster generating function
entries.text: Let H(s)= {n 1} {P}( C 0 =n)\,s^n be the generating function of the open cluster of the root. The root contributes s; each child branch contributes either nothing (edge closed, factor 1-p) or a cluster with generating function H(s) (edge open, factor p\,H(s)). Independence over children gives the functional equation Setting s=1 recovers (22.2), since u=H(1) is the probability that the cluster is finite. Differentiating at s=1 and writing =H'(1) gives in agreement with (22.5). At p=p c, for a finite-variance offspring law, the equation has a double root at s=1, and a standard singularity analysis of (22.6) gives Comparing with the definitions {P}( C 0 =n) n^{-1-1/ } and n s s^{- } gives =2 and =5/2, the mean-field values. The square-root singularity is the tree's substitute for a phase transition with a divergent correlation length: there is no length scale at all, only a generation count.

entries.chapterTitle: Trees, generating functions, and message passing
entries.heading: 22.3 Sparse graphs and the local tree limit
entries.text: The configuration model fixes a degree sequence (k 1, ,k N) with i k i=2M and pairs the 2M stubs uniformly at random. Choose a vertex uniformly and look at its neighbourhood out to a fixed radius r. With probability tending to one as N , that neighbourhood is a tree, and the root has offspring distribution the size-biased law: a neighbour of a random vertex has one edge already used, and its remaining k edges are distributed as q k. The convergence is the local weak convergence of Benjamini and Schramm (2001); a textbook treatment is in van der Hofstad (2017). Local convergence is not enough to determine a global event such as percolation on {Z}^d. It is enough for the configuration model because the giant component is created by a branching instability, and the cycles that would correct the branching count are rare at the scale of the emerging component. Under a finite-second-moment condition, the Molloy–Reed criterion is exact: a giant component exists iff Durrett (2007) and Janson, Łuczak and Ruciński (2000) give the precise statements and the critical-window behaviour.

entries.chapterTitle: Trees, generating functions, and message passing
entries.heading: 22.4 The generating-function solution of the configuration model
entries.text: Let be the degree generating function and its size-biased counterpart. Add bond percolation with retention T (the letter p is reserved for the occupation probability of the lattice chapters; T is the transmissibility of Chapter 23). Define u as the probability that a vertex reached by following an edge is not connected to the giant component through that edge. Its k-1 other edges are distributed as G 1; each is either not retained (probability 1-T) or retained and fails to continue (probability T u). Therefore The probability that the root is not in the giant component is the same expression with the root's degree law G 0: Equation (22.9) is the standard configuration-model solution (Newman 2002); it is exact in the limit N under the same finite-second-moment conditions as Molloy–Reed. Threshold. Linearise (22.8) at u=1: the derivative of the right side is T\,G 1'(1), and A nontrivial solution appears when T( -1) 1, i.e. At T=1 this is the Molloy–Reed condition 2. Equation (22.10) is the same threshold derived in Chapter 10 by a first-moment argument; the generating function supplies the giant-component size as well. Erdős–Rényi check. For Poisson degrees with mean c, G 0(x)=G 1(x)=e^{c(x-1)}, so (22.9) becomes The nonzero solution is the familiar giant component of the random graph; at cT=2 it is S=0.7968 . Scale-free check. For p k k^{- { {deg}}} with 2< { {deg}} 3, k^2 = in the infinite-size limit, so = and T c=0. The statement is about the limit; a finite network has a cutoff and a small but positive threshold. Chapter 10 discusses the finite-size qualification.

entries.chapterTitle: Trees, generating functions, and message passing
entries.heading: 22.5 Message passing on a fixed graph
entries.text: The generating-function solution assumes a degree distribution, not a specific graph. For a given finite graph with adjacency i, define the cavity message u {i j} as the probability that i is not connected to the giant component through any neighbour other than j. The neighbours of i other than j are independent if the graph is a tree , so and the probability that i is outside the giant component is On a tree, (22.11)–(22.12) are exact and can be solved by one pass from the leaves inward. On a graph with cycles they are the Bethe approximation : the product assumes that the branches behind different neighbours are independent given i, which fails when short loops connect them. The error is governed by the density of short loops, not by the system size. Karrer and Newman (2010) use exactly this system for general epidemic models, and Mézard and Montanari (2009) develop the cavity method in general. The message-passing form is what makes the tree calculation useful on real data: a contact network is given, the degree distribution is not, and (22.11) can be iterated on the actual adjacency in O(m) time per sweep. The reference implementation is messagePassingPercolation / message passing percolation, with a prefix/suffix product and a mate array for the opposite half-edge.

entries.chapterTitle: Trees, generating functions, and message passing
entries.heading: 22.6 What trees get right, and what they do not
entries.text: The Bethe lattice is the d limit, and its threshold 1/(z-1) is not the threshold of {Z}^d with the same degree. Table 22.1 makes the gap visible. Graph z Tree prediction 1/(z-1) Actual p c (bond) Status --- --- --- --- --- {Z}^2 4 1/3=0.3333 1/2 exact (Kesten) Simple cubic {Z}^3 6 1/5=0.2 0.24881182(10) numerical z-regular tree z 1/(z-1) 1/(z-1) exact Configuration model k 1/( -1) 1/( -1) exact, N Table 22.1. The tree value is exact on trees and on the configuration model, and it is a lower bound on {Z}^d that gets worse as d falls. The reason is that a tree has no cycles to block a would-be infinite cluster: on {Z}^2, the dual closed crossings that enforce p c=1/2 have no tree analogue. The configuration model is different again: it is tree-like at the scale of the giant component, so the branching answer is asymptotically exact even though the graph is finite and has cycles. This distinction is the most common source of error in applied work. A "Bethe approximation" to a two-dimensional material is not a controlled approximation; a Bethe approximation to a sparse contact network can be asymptotically exact for the giant component and is usually a good approximation for the threshold, but the size of the error is a property of the particular graph, not a universal constant.

entries.chapterTitle: Trees, generating functions, and message passing
entries.heading: 22.7 Worked checks
entries.text: Three numbers are worth carrying in memory. Bethe, z=3, p=1/2. Equation (22.4) is u=(1/2+u/2)^2, i.e. (u-1)^2=0. The double root at u=1 is the critical point: =0 and the two branches merge. At p=0.6 the roots are u=1 and u=4/9, and Erdős–Rényi, c=2, T=1. S=1-e^{-2S} has the nonzero root S=0.796812 ; the threshold is at c=1, and the giant component at c=2 occupies about four fifths of the graph. Poisson tree, c=2, p=0.6. Here p c=1/2, so the tree is supercritical; the nonzero solution of u=e^{-cp(1-u)}=e^{-1.2(1-u)} gives =1-u=0.313698 . This is exactly the Erdős–Rényi giant component at cT=1.2, because a Poisson degree distribution is stable under thinning: the root has {Poisson}(2p)= {Poisson}(1.2) open children, the same law as every forward branch. The agreement is a useful check on both calculations, and it is special to Poisson degrees. The four-language libraries implement these three checks as bethePercolation, configurationGiantComponent and the fixed-point solver behind (22.9); the regression values are in the test suites.

entries.chapterTitle: Trees, generating functions, and message passing
entries.heading: 22.8 What to carry away
entries.text: 1. On a tree, percolation is a branching process. The recursion (22.1) and the threshold (22.3) are exact, not approximations. 2. Generating functions turn the recursion into algebra. The cluster generating function (22.6) gives the mean size, the critical exponent =2 and the n^{-3/2} tail in one calculation. 3. Sparse graphs inherit the tree answer globally. The configuration-model equations (22.9)–(22.10) are exact in the N limit, under a finite-second-moment condition. 4. On a lattice, the tree answer is only a local limit. The cycles that the tree omits are exactly what fixes p c=1/2 in two dimensions, and what makes the three-dimensional threshold larger than 1/(2d-1). 5. Message passing is the finite-graph version. It is exact on trees, asymptotically exact on locally tree-like graphs, and a controlled approximation elsewhere only when the short-loop density is small. Chapter 23 uses these equations for the final size of an epidemic, where T is a transmission probability rather than a bond occupancy.

entries.heading: Epidemics as percolation
entries.text: An SIR epidemic and bond percolation answer the same question when the question is who is ever infected . The answer is exact, not an analogy: retain each contact edge with the probability that it transmits, and the ever-infected set is the open cluster of the initial case. That identity gives the final size, the epidemic threshold, and the vaccination target in one calculation. It says nothing about the peak, the time course, or the effect of behaviour — and most failed applications fail by forgetting the second sentence.

entries.heading: 23.1 The mapping, stated precisely
entries.text: Consider an SIR process on a static contact graph G=(V,E) with one initially infectious vertex. Each infectious vertex i has an infectious period i, and while infectious it makes contacts with each susceptible neighbour at rate . The number of transmissions along an edge is then Poisson with mean i (if the contacts are a Poisson process), so the edge transmits with probability If the infectious periods are independent and identically distributed, condition on them. Each directed edge i j is open independently with probability 1-e^{- i}, and the set of vertices that ever become infected is the out-component of the initial case in this directed random graph. On a tree, each edge is traversed only away from the initial case, so averaging over the infectious periods gives independent edge retention with probability In the configuration-model limit the same reduction holds because cycles are negligible at the scale of the giant out-component. This is the mapping used below; on a general graph with short cycles the exact object is the directed out-component, and the undirected percolation cluster is the tree approximation. Two special cases are worth recording. For a constant infectious period , T=1-e^{- }. For a Markovian SIR with recovery rate (mean infectious period 1/ ) and transmission rate , T= /( + ). The mapping requires the contacts to be independent across edges; that is what makes the percolation representation exact, and it is the assumption that temporal and behavioural heterogeneity violate. For several initial cases, the final set is the union of their open clusters. In a large population with a vanishing initial fraction, the final size is the giant component whenever the parameters are supercritical; near the threshold the fluctuation of the initial seed matters.

entries.heading: 23.2 The final-size equation
entries.text: Take the configuration model of Chapter 22 with degree generating functions G 0 and G 1. The bond-percolation solution (22.9) with retention T gives the final fraction directly: The derivation is the message-passing one: a vertex escapes infection if every neighbour either does not transmit (probability 1-T) or transmits to a neighbour whose own branch dies out (probability T u). The giant component is the set of vertices that do not escape. For Poisson degrees with mean c, G 0=G 1=e^{c(x-1)} and (23.1) collapses to the scalar equation The trivial solution R =0 always exists. A positive solution exists iff R 0 1, and then it is unique. The same bifurcation is the percolation threshold of Chapter 22: Equation (23.3) is the quantitative content of "the epidemic threshold is a percolation threshold". It is exact in the configuration-model limit; on a real finite network it is the leading term of a 1/ k expansion. Worked values. For R 0=2, (23.2) gives R =0.7968 ; for R 0=3, R =0.9405 ; for R 0=1.5, R =0.5828 . The approach to R =1 is slow: even R 0=5 leaves about 0.7\% susceptible. These are arithmetic consequences of the mean-field equation, not estimates for a particular pathogen.

entries.heading: 23.3 Herd immunity
entries.text: Suppose a fraction v of the population is immunised at random before the epidemic. In the configuration model, immunisation removes vertices and all their edges.
